title: Urban forest strategy and Sugarbush South housing plan
subtitle: Water meter contract, a Hemlock Street tower public meeting, and Erbsville Road by-laws also featured.
overview: Council sent the draft Urban Forest Management Strategy out for a final round of public consultation {{vote:m3}}. Staff said they aim to bring a final version back in June. Council also awarded the residential water meter supply tender and approved a reserve transfer to help fund it {{vote:m4}}.

Council approved the Sugarbush South land use plan, which includes an official plan amendment, zoning changes and urban design guidelines. These enable mid-rise "missing middle" housing in the neighbourhood {{vote:m5}}. Council also passed by-laws enacting the Erbsville Road official plan amendment and rezoning that it had approved on March 30 {{vote:m6}}.

An informal public meeting was held on a proposed tall residential building on Hemlock Street. No decision was made, and staff will report back later. Council met in closed session to receive legal advice about water infrastructure, and the minutes report no public outcome.

decisions.detail: Council approved the report and directed staff to circulate the draft strategy to interested parties and post it on Engage Waterloo for final consultation and feedback.
Council awarded the supply and delivery of residential water meters (RFT26-09, Stream 2) to KTI Limited for a total of $1,275,212.82 including unrecoverable HST.
Council approved a $445,000 transfer from the City Utilities Water Stabilization Reserve to the Water Meter Replacement capital project.
Council approved Official Plan Amendment No. 70, Zoning By-law Amendment Z-25-19 and the Sugarbush South Urban Design Guidelines.

debate: On the urban forest strategy, several councillors raised concerns about a proposed private tree by-law. They cited neighbour-to-neighbour disputes, the risk that it could discourage people from planting trees, and the cost of an enforcement position. Consultants said such by-laws are common in comparable municipalities and work best paired with incentives.

Councillors asked for finer tree equity work, including ward-by-ward measures and protection for mature canopy where overhead hydro lines conflict with trees. Staff said tree equity was added mid-project and is an early step. They said tree protection during city projects has improved but enforcement is mostly reactive.

On Sugarbush South, one councillor argued that intentions to protect existing trees are not enough and asked about a tree protection area. Another asked how the zoning would produce a range of unit sizes rather than one building type. Staff pointed to larger front setbacks, lot consolidation, and a parking rate not tied to bedroom count.

A resident speaking on Sugarbush South said past tree replacement promises were not kept. The resident also worried that provincial changes limit the city's ability to require sustainable design. Staff said they would comment to the province and keep pressing developers where they can.

On the Hemlock Street proposal, councillors asked whether going well above the 12-storey limit and the density cap would set a precedent for Northdale, and noted the area plan came from extensive community consultation. The applicant's team said the narrow tower allows larger family-sized units, and staff will review the height question.
